scenes.text: May twenty seventh, nineteen ninety one. Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Three women find a fourteen year old boy in the street, undressed and bleeding, and they call the police.

marks.label: Three women report a boy in the street

scenes.cap: Three women called. The police came.

scenes.text: Two officers arrive. A man tells them the boy is nineteen, and his boyfriend, and that this is a domestic argument.

kinetic.sub: the account given to responding officers

scenes.text: The boy is not nineteen. He is fourteen. And the man is on probation, at that moment, for sexually assaulting a thirteen year old boy three years earlier.
The officers hand the boy back to him. In the words of a published appeals court opinion, they released Sinthasomphone, who was a minor, into Dahmer's care.
scenes.source: Balcerzak v. Board of Fire and Police Commissioners, Wis. Ct. App. No. 98-2889
scenes.cap: “…released Sinthasomphone, who was a minor, into Dahmer's care.”

scenes.text: The next sentence of that opinion is seven words long. Dahmer murdered Sinthasomphone shortly thereafter.
scenes.source: Balcerzak v. Board of Fire and Police Commissioners — the court's own words

scenes.text: This film is not about what Jeffrey Dahmer did. That has been told a thousand times, and it needs no retelling. This is about the documents that came afterward, and what they show a system will forgive.
To understand the night of May twenty seventh, you have to start in nineteen eighty eight, with a different boy and the same surname.
In nineteen eighty eight, Dahmer was arrested for drugging and sexually assaulting a thirteen year old boy named Somsack Sinthasomphone. He was convicted.
He was not sent to prison for it. He was placed on probation.

Three years later, still on that probation, he was standing in a Milwaukee street explaining to two officers that the fourteen year old beside him was an adult. That fourteen year old was Somsack's younger brother, Konerak.

scenes.chapter:
Chapter two
What the officers did
scenes.text: What happened in the next twenty minutes is described, dryly, in a court record.
The opinion says the officers conducted a brief investigation. It says they released a minor into the care of the man who had just been found with him in the street.
scenes.source: Wis. Ct. App. No. 98-2889 — statement of facts

scenes.text: It does not say they knew what he was. There is nothing in this record that says they knew, and this film will not pretend otherwise.
What the record does establish is that a fourteen year old was handed back, and that a police department later concluded its own rules had been broken in the process.
In July of nineteen ninety one, Dahmer was arrested, and what had happened that night in May became public.
The then chief of police discharged the officers involved, for violating department rules during that investigation.
scenes.source: Wis. Ct. App. No. 98-2889 — discharge and appeal history

scenes.text: The officers appealed to the city's Fire and Police Commission. The commission upheld the discharges.
scenes.source: Wis. Ct. App. No. 98-2889 — “the FPC, which upheld their discharges”
scenes.cap: The commission agreed with the chief.

scenes.text: At that point, in the eyes of both the department and its civilian oversight body, the matter was settled. It was not settled.
What happened next was not a jury, and not a public argument about policing. It was a section number.
Wisconsin statute sixty two point fifty governs how a police officer may be discharged, suspended, or reduced in rank, and what a court must do when it reviews that decision.
scenes.source: Wis. Stat. § 62.50, as construed in Wis. Ct. App. No. 98-2889

scenes.text: The statute is narrow, and it is procedural. It says that where the accused is not permanently discharged, the officer shall be immediately reinstated in his or her former position.
On review, the discharges were vacated and converted into suspensions. Under the statute, that meant reinstatement, and it meant back pay.
scenes.source: Wis. Ct. App. No. 98-2889 — discharges vacated, officers reinstated

scenes.text: Reported at roughly fifty five thousand dollars each.
That is the whole mechanism. Not a finding that the officers had acted properly. A statute about the difference between a discharge and a suspension.
What happened after the reinstatement is the part of this record that almost nobody has read, and it is the part that says the most.

The circuit court that reviewed the discharges called them unreasonable discipline. It sent the matter back, suggesting that a suspension of not more than sixty days would, in its words, more appropriately serve the ends of justice.
scenes.source: Wis. Ct. App. No. 98-2889 — circuit court remand
scenes.cap: “…more appropriately serve the ends of justice.”

scenes.text: Sixty days is not an arbitrary number. It is the ceiling written into the statute. Under section sixty two point fifty, a board that sustains the charges may discharge an officer permanently, or suspend without pay for a period not exceeding sixty days.
So the commission vacated the discharges and imposed the maximum the law allowed. Sixty days without pay.

kinetic.sub: the statutory maximum, imposed instead of discharge

scenes.text: And then the argument moved to what the word days means.

kinetic.sub: the question the case turned on

scenes.text: The police department applied the suspension the way it always had. Sixty consecutive workdays, effective the twenty seventh of November, nineteen ninety two.
scenes.source: Wis. Ct. App. No. 98-2889 — “sixty (60) consecutive workdays effective 11-27-92”

scenes.text: The officer appealed that too. And the circuit court agreed with him, holding that days meant calendar days, and ordering the commission to redefine the suspension as sixty calendar days, with any lost rights restored.
scenes.source: Wis. Ct. App. No. 98-2889 — summary judgment for Balcerzak

scenes.text: Working days, or calendar days. Roughly twelve weeks, or roughly eight. That difference is what the litigation was about.

marks.label: How the department applied the suspension
What the circuit court ordered instead

scenes.text: The Court of Appeals reversed, and held the department had it right. Sixty working days.
scenes.source: Wis. Ct. App. No. 98-2889 — holding; suspension applied to working days

scenes.text: Nineteen pages of statutory construction. A published opinion of a state appeals court. Filed in the year two thousand, about a night in nineteen ninety one.

Nowhere in those nineteen pages does anyone argue about whether handing a fourteen year old boy back was wrong. That question was settled early, and quietly, and then everything after it was about arithmetic.

scenes.chapter:
Chapter six
What was said about it
scenes.text: The reinstatement was criticised immediately, and the criticism was specific.

Many argued the investigation that night had been cursory because Konerak was not white, and because the officers accepted, without checking, that he was an adult in a relationship with the man beside him.
That is a criticism, widely made, and it belongs in the record as exactly that. No court finding in these documents declares it as fact, and this film will not upgrade an accusation into a verdict.
Konerak's family sued the city in federal court. The case is reported as Estate of Sinthasomphone against the City of Milwaukee, decided in nineteen ninety two.
The civil side ran in parallel. Konerak's estate sued the city in federal court, and the reported decisions in that litigation span from nineteen ninety two into nineteen ninety five.

We are not showing you those opinions, because we could not obtain clean copies of them for this episode. They exist, they are cited as Estate of Sinthasomphone against the City of Milwaukee, and when we have them, they will be on screen.
That is the rule on this channel. If we cannot put the document in front of you, we tell you it is missing rather than filling the gap with something that looks like it.
Dahmer's own case moved faster than any of it.
He was charged with fifteen counts of murder. His defence did not dispute that he had killed. It argued that he was insane.
On February fifteenth, nineteen ninety two, after roughly five hours, the jury rejected that argument and found him guilty on all fifteen counts.
Two days later he was sentenced to fifteen consecutive life terms. In November of nineteen ninety four, he was killed by another inmate in prison.

marks.label: Guilty on 15 counts, insanity plea rejected

scenes.text: So here is the record, in one sentence. A man on probation for assaulting a thirteen year old was handed that boy's fourteen year old brother by two uniformed officers, and the paperwork that followed put those officers back on the payroll with back pay.
Every step of that sentence is in a filing you can read. None of it required a secret.

kinetic.sub: every document in this episode is public

scenes.text: Three women called the police that night, and they were right about what they saw. The system's own paperwork is the part that failed.

This is Criminal Record, where every case is built from the primary record and nothing else. If this one held you, the file we opened before it is a case where four students died and the record still contains no motive. Subscribe, and both are waiting.
